claims.source: Study of cortical functional connectivity also has revealed fine-grained topographies in the connectome (Arcaro et al., 2015; Haak et al., 2018; Heinzle et al., 2011; Jbabdi et al., 2013)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on functional connectivity.

claims.claim: Fine-grained topographies in the connectome are closely related to patterns of activity.
claims.source: Study of cortical functional connectivity also has revealed fine-grained topographies in the connectome (Arcaro et al., 2015; Haak et al., 2018; Heinzle et al., 2011; Jbabdi et al., 2013) that are closely related to these patterns of activity (Guntupalli et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Guntupalli et al., 2018.

claims.claim: The surface structure of functional cortical topographies shows considerable variability across individual brains for encoding the same information.
claims.source: The surface structure of functional cortical topographies, however, shows considerable variability across individual brains for encoding the same information (Cox and Savoy, 2003; Guntupalli et al., 2016; Haxby et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research demonstrating inter-individual variability.

claims.claim: Hyperalignment derives from the term hyperspace to convey the paradigm shift from modeling cortical functional architecture in a three-dimensional anatomical space to modeling the information encoded in functional architecture in a high-dimensional information space.
claims.source: Hyperalignment derives from the term hyperspace, to convey the paradigm shift from modeling cortical functional architecture in a three-dimensional anatomical space to modeling the information encoded in functional architecture in a high-dimensional information space.
claims.evidence: This explains the etymology and conceptual motivation for the term 'hyperalignment'.

claims.claim: The common information space captures the 'deep structure' of shared information that is encoded in the variable 'surface structure' of idiosyncratic topographies in individual brains.
claims.source: This common information space captures the 'deep structure' of shared information that is encoded in the variable 'surface structure' of idiosyncratic topographies in individual brains.
claims.evidence: This is a conceptual claim about the nature of the common model space, supported by the overall framework and results.

claims.claim: Information is contained in the relationships among pattern vectors – distinctions and similarities.
claims.source: Information is contained in the relationships among pattern vectors – distinctions and similarities – and these relationships are preserved when the space is transformed from an individual cortical space to the common information space.
claims.evidence: This defines how information is operationalized in the hyperalignment framework.

claims.claim: In hyperalignment transformations, the features that define the space in individual brains are remixed to support the same information structure with shared basis functions.
claims.source: In these transformations, the features that define the space in individual brains – response tuning functions and connectivity profiles – are remixed to support the same information structure with shared basis functions.
claims.evidence: This describes a key property of the transformation matrices derived through hyperalignment.

claims.claim: Shared information is decomposed into overlapping basis functions that are instantiated in individual brains with idiosyncratic topographies.
claims.source: Shared information is decomposed into overlapping basis functions that are instantiated in individual brains with idiosyncratic topographies.
claims.evidence: This describes the computational model of cortical functional architecture proposed by hyperalignment.

claims.claim: Cortical patterns of activity and connectivity are modeled as mixtures of topographic basis functions.
claims.source: Cortical patterns of activity and connectivity are modeled as mixtures of these topographic basis functions.
claims.evidence: This describes how individual cortical patterns are represented in the hyperalignment framework.

claims.claim: The topographic information embedded in the model's shared bases is not strongly constrained by areal boundaries.
claims.source: Our common model accounts for coarse areal structure insofar as the model's shared basis set for fine-scale topographies can be mixed to identify the boundaries for functional areas in individual brains, but the topographic information embedded in the model's shared bases is not strongly constrained by these areal boundaries
claims.evidence: This is supported by analyses showing that areal boundaries account for only a small portion of variance in the model.

claims.claim: Areal structure may play a smaller role in how information is organized in cortex than was previously believed.
claims.source: the topographic information embedded in the model's shared bases is not strongly constrained by these areal boundaries, suggesting that areal structure may play a smaller role in how information is organized in cortex than was previously believed.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that areal boundaries do not strongly constrain the model's basis functions.

claims.claim: For fMRI data, local pattern elements are typically voxels or vertices on the cortical surface.
claims.source: For fMRI data, local pattern elements are typically voxels (or vertices on the cortical surface).
claims.evidence: This is a standard description of fMRI data structure.

claims.claim: The relevance of the hyperalignment conceptual framework for modeling cortical functional architecture is not specific to any measurement modality or neural variable.
claims.source: The relevance of the hyperalignment conceptual framework for modeling cortical functional architecture is not specific to any measurement modality or neural variable
claims.evidence: This is supported by examples of applying hyperalignment to different modalities and even artificial neural networks.

claims.claim: The computational procedures of hyperalignment can be applied to data matrices obtained with other measurement modalities.
claims.source: the computational procedures can also be applied to data matrices obtained with other measurement modalities (e.g. Chen et al., 2020) or even artificial neural networks (Lu et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to work applying hyperalignment to other data types.

claims.claim: The row vectors in data matrices serve as indices of the brain state corresponding to a given stimulus or cognitive state.
claims.source: The row vectors may be patterns of activity at different points in time or response patterns recovered from multiple instances of a given event or experimental manipulation (using trial averaging or deconvolution) and serve as indices of the brain state corresponding to a given stimulus or cognitive state.
claims.evidence: This describes how row vectors in the data matrix are interpreted.

claims.claim: Information is defined as relationships among functional pattern vectors, typically quantified as the similarity or dissimilarity between each pair of vectors.
claims.source: Here, we define 'information' as relationships among functional pattern vectors, typically quantified as the similarity (or dissimilarity/distance) between each pair of vectors (Connolly et al., 2012; Connolly et al., 2011; Edelman et al., 1998; Hanson et al., 2004; Kriegeskorte et al., 2008a; Kriegeskorte and Kievit, 2013; O'Toole et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is a formal definition supported by citations to prior work using this framework.

claims.claim: Vectors that are more similar to each other are located nearer to each other in vector space.
claims.source: These dissimilarities index the distinctiveness of each vector relative to other vectors; vectors that are more similar to each other are located nearer to each other in vector space.
claims.evidence: This is a basic property of vector space geometry.

claims.claim: The geometric framework for operationalizing information as the relationships among distributed patterns in a vector space is used in a variety of fields.
claims.source: This geometric framework for operationalizing information as the relationships among distributed patterns in a vector space is used in a variety of fields, including psychology (e.g. Edelman, 1998; Shepard, 1987), information retrieval (e.g. Salton et al., 1975), and natural language processing (e.g. Deerwester et al., 1990).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to work in multiple fields.

claims.claim: The vector geometry of information in cortical spaces is highly similar across brains.
claims.source: The vector geometry of information in cortical spaces is highly similar across brains (Connolly et al., 2016; Connolly et al., 2012; Connolly et al., 2011; Diedrichsen and Kriegeskorte, 2017; Guntupalli et al., 2018; Guntupalli et al., 2016; Kriegeskorte and Kievit, 2013; Nastase et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claims.claim: Hyperalignment leverages the inter-individual similarity of vector geometry to create a shared information space that minimizes differences between corresponding vectors across individuals while preserving vector geometry.
claims.source: Hyperalignment leverages the inter-individual similarity of vector geometry to create a shared information space that minimizes differences between corresponding vectors across individuals while preserving vector geometry.
claims.evidence: This describes the computational strategy of hyperalignment.

claims.claim: The columns of data matrices in the common model space are the coordinate axes or dimensions for that information space.
claims.source: The columns of data matrices in the common model space are the coordinate axes or dimensions for that information space.
claims.evidence: This describes the structure of the common model space data matrix.

claims.claim: The dimensions in the common model space are weighted sums of nearby anatomical locations in individual brains.
claims.source: The dimensions in the common model space are no longer anatomical locations but, rather, are weighted sums of nearby anatomical locations in individual brains
claims.evidence: This describes how model dimensions relate to anatomical locations.

claims.claim: The transformations are not a one-to-one mapping from cortical loci to common space dimensions.
claims.source: the transformations are not a one-to-one mapping from cortical loci to common space dimensions.
claims.evidence: This is a property of the transformation matrices.

claims.claim: The distribution of transformation weights is specific to each brain.
claims.source: The distribution of these weights is specific to each brain.
claims.evidence: This describes the individual-specific nature of transformation matrices.

claims.claim: The number of dimensions in the common space can differ from the number of cortical loci in the data matrices from which the space is derived.
claims.source: The number of dimensions in the common space (m in Figure 2) can differ from the number of cortical loci in the data matrices (k in Figure 2) from which the space is derived.
claims.evidence: This describes a property of the common model space implementation.

claims.claim: In some implementations, the number of model dimensions matches the number of cortical loci in a 'reference brain'.
claims.source: In some implementations, the number of model dimensions matches the number of cortical loci in a 'reference brain', allowing patterns in the model space to be illustrated in the reference brain anatomy (Guntupalli et al., 2018; Guntupalli et al., 2016; Haxby et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This describes one implementation approach, supported by citations.

claims.claim: In some implementations, the model space is reduced to capture shared information in a smaller number of dimensions and reduce noise or overfitting.
claims.source: In other implementations, the model space is reduced to capture shared information in a smaller number of dimensions and reduce noise or overfitting (Chen et al., 2015; Guntupalli et al., 2016; Haxby et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This describes another implementation approach, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The coordinate axes for the common information space can be arbitrarily rotated, preserving vector geometry while altering the response tuning and connectivity profiles for the coordinate axes.
claims.source: The coordinate axes for that space – the model dimensions – carry information in the form of shared functional profiles (response tuning vectors or functional connectivity vectors), but they can be arbitrarily rotated, preserving vector geometry while altering the response tuning and connectivity profiles for the coordinate axes.
claims.evidence: This is a mathematical property of the vector space representation.

claims.claim: The Procrustes transformation is the orthogonal matrix that minimizes the distances between two matrices of paired vectors with a rigid rotation.
claims.source: The Procrustes transformation is the orthogonal matrix that minimizes the distances between two matrices of paired vectors with a rigid rotation, which is 'improper' in that it allows reflections as well as rotations.
claims.evidence: This is a mathematical definition of the Procrustes transformation.

claims.claim: Generalized Procrustes Analysis finds transformation matrices for a group of data matrices that minimize distances by iteratively aligning each new matrix to the mean of previously aligned matrices.
claims.source: GPA finds transformation matrices for a group of data matrices that minimize distances by iteratively aligning each new matrix to the mean of previously aligned matrices.
claims.evidence: This describes the GPA algorithm.

claims.claim: A rigid rotation preserves all pairwise distances between pattern vectors within each original matrix.
claims.source: A rigid rotation preserves all pairwise distances between pattern vectors within each original matrix.
claims.evidence: This is a mathematical property of rigid rotations.

claims.claim: Local vector geometry is highly correlated across brains.
claims.source: We and others have shown that local vector geometry is highly correlated across brains (Connolly et al., 2016; Connolly et al., 2012; Connolly et al., 2011; Guntupalli et al., 2018; Guntupalli et al., 2016; Kriegeskorte and Kievit, 2013; Nastase et al., 2017)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: Local vector geometry is a key feature of shared information structure.
claims.source: We and others have shown that local vector geometry is highly correlated across brains (Connolly et al., 2016; Connolly et al., 2012; Connolly et al., 2011; Guntupalli et al., 2018; Guntupalli et al., 2016; Kriegeskorte and Kievit, 2013; Nastase et al., 2017), indicating that it is a key feature of shared information structure (Diedrichsen and Kriegeskorte, 2017; Ejaz et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is an inference supported by citations.

claims.claim: Hyperalignment algorithms that mostly preserve vector geometry tend to generalize better to novel data than algorithms that do not.
claims.source: Hyperalignment algorithms that mostly preserve vector geometry tend to generalize better to novel data than algorithms that do not (Xu et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Xu et al., 2012.

claims.claim: Whole-cortex searchlight hyperalignment makes local models in overlapping searchlights that cover the cortex, then aggregates the local transformation matrices into a whole-cortex transformation matrix.
claims.source: Whole-cortex searchlight hyperalignment, by contrast, makes local models in overlapping searchlights (Kriegeskorte et al., 2006; Oosterhof et al., 2011) that cover the cortex, then aggregates the local transformation matrices into a whole-cortex transformation matrix, thereby mostly preserving local vector geometry (Guntupalli et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This describes the searchlight hyperalignment algorithm.

claims.claim: Data are aligned anatomically to a standard cortical surface prior to whole-cortex searchlight hyperalignment.
claims.source: Data are aligned anatomically to a standard cortical surface (e.g., FreeSurfer's fsaverage; Fischl et al., 1999) prior to whole-cortex searchlight hyperalignment.
claims.evidence: This describes a preprocessing step in the hyperalignment procedure.

claims.claim: The cortical fields for local basis functions are overlapping and constrained only by searchlight size, not by areal boundaries.
claims.source: The cortical fields for local basis functions, defined by the voxels with nonzero weights in columns of the whole-cortex transformation matrices, are overlapping and constrained only by searchlight size, not by areal boundaries.
claims.evidence: This describes a property of the basis functions derived from searchlight hyperalignment.

claims.claim: A cortical field in the common information space produced by whole-cortex hyperalignment is only defined insofar as it is instantiated in the idiosyncratic cortical topography of an individual brain.
claims.source: A cortical field of contiguous cortical vertices, such as a searchlight or ROI, in the common information space produced by whole-cortex hyperalignment is only defined insofar as it is instantiated in the idiosyncratic cortical topography of an individual brain.
claims.evidence: This describes a conceptual property of cortical fields in the common model space.

claims.claim: Reducing the dimensionality of the common model space using principal component analysis can preserve or even improve performance, as indexed with between-subject multivariate pattern classification.
claims.source: We have shown that reducing the dimensionality of the common model space using principal component analysis (PCA; Guntupalli et al., 2016; Haxby et al., 2011) can preserve or even improve performance, as indexed with between-subject multivariate pattern classification (bsMVPC; Guntupalli et al., 2016; Haxby et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: Between-subject MVPC accuracies can be substantially higher with lower dimensional models.
claims.source: Later work suggests that bsMVPC accuracies can be substantially higher with lower dimensional models (Chen et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Dimensionality reduction necessarily warps vector geometry but can effectively denoise data in common space by discarding lower-order eigenvectors.
claims.source: Dimensionality reduction necessarily warps vector geometry but can effectively denoise data in common space by discarding lower-order eigenvectors.
claims.evidence: This describes a trade-off in dimensionality reduction.

claims.claim: With regularized CCA, a small relaxation of the orthogonality constraint enhances performance, as indexed with between-subject multivariate pattern classification.
claims.source: With regularized CCA we find that a small relaxation of the orthogonality constraint enhances performance, as indexed with between-subject multivariate pattern classification (bsMVPC).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the authors' work with rCCA.

claims.claim: The human connectome has fine-grained topographies that are not captured by mean connections between areas.
claims.source: Previous work has shown that the human connectome has fine-grained topographies that are not captured by mean connections between areas (Arcaro et al., 2015; Braga et al., 2019; Haak et al., 2018; Heinzle et al., 2011; Jbabdi et al., 2013)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: Connectivity hyperalignment has shown that fine-scale structure in the connectome is prevalent across all of cortex and of higher dimensionality than can be captured with known topographies.
claims.source: connectivity hyperalignment has shown that this fine-scale structure in the connectome is prevalent across all of cortex and of higher dimensionality than can be captured with known topographies, such as retinotopy and orientation selectivity (Guntupalli et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Guntupalli et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Connectivity hyperalignment does not require a common stimulus paradigm, affording hyperalignment of resting state data.
claims.source: Whereas response hyperalignment depends on response pattern vectors in experimental data that are locked to stimuli, connectivity hyperalignment depends on connectivity vectors for a defined set of connectivity targets and does not require a common stimulus paradigm, affording hyperalignment of resting state data (Guntupalli et al., 2018) or across different experiments (Nastase et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This describes an advantage of connectivity hyperalignment, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Transformation matrices derived with connectivity hyperalignment can be applied to response data, effectively aligning response pattern vectors.
claims.source: Transformation matrices derived with connectivity hyperalignment can be applied to response data, effectively aligning response pattern vectors (Guntupalli et al., 2018; Nastase et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claims.claim: Response hyperalignment aligns connectivity information and connectivity hyperalignment aligns population response information.
claims.source: Validation tests show that response hyperalignment aligns connectivity information and connectivity hyperalignment aligns population response information.
claims.evidence: This is supported by validation tests described in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Estimating the parameters to transform high-dimensional spaces from individual brains into a common high-dimensional space requires a rich set of data that samples a wide variety of cortical patterns.
claims.source: Estimating the parameters to transform high-dimensional spaces from individual brains into a common high-dimensional space requires a rich set of data that samples a wide variety of cortical patterns in order to generalize to novel stimuli or tasks.
claims.evidence: This is a requirement for effective hyperalignment, supported by empirical results.

claims.claim: A common model space based on transformation matrices derived from responses to naturalistic audiovisual movies has general validity across a variety of experiments.
claims.source: We have shown that a common model space based on transformation matrices derived from responses to naturalistic audiovisual movies has general validity across a variety of experiments (Guntupalli et al., 2016; Haxby et al., 2011; Nastase et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: Transformation matrices estimated from controlled experiments with a limited set of stimuli or cognitive states do not generalize well to other contexts or paradigms.
claims.source: By contrast, transformation matrices estimated from controlled experiments with a limited set of stimuli or cognitive states may suffice for that experiment, but do not generalize well to other contexts or paradigms (Haxby et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Haxby et al., 2011.

claims.claim: Naturalistic movie stimuli evoke a rich variety of brain states involving multiple coordinated systems.
claims.source: Such stimuli evoke a rich variety of brain states involving multiple coordinated systems for visual and auditory perception, perception of dynamic action, narrative, and speech, memory, attention, semantic knowledge, and social cognition.
claims.evidence: This describes properties of naturalistic movie stimuli.

claims.claim: Movies are engineered to be engaging and guide attention.
claims.source: Movies are engineered to be engaging and guide attention.
claims.evidence: This is a general property of movie stimuli.

claims.claim: Movies build a rich set of expectations for upcoming stimuli and events affording strong predictions.
claims.source: Movies also build a rich set of expectations for upcoming stimuli and events affording strong predictions (and prediction errors).
claims.evidence: This describes a property of movie stimuli relevant to neural processing.

claims.claim: Controlled experiments typically randomize trial order, deliberately decontextualizing each event and providing no basis for accurate prediction.
claims.source: Controlled experiments, on the other hand, typically randomize trial order, deliberately decontextualizing each event and providing no basis for accurate prediction.
claims.evidence: This describes a typical property of controlled experiments.

claims.claim: Between-subject multivariate pattern classification accuracies in ventral temporal extrastriate visual cortex for naturalistic, dynamic stimuli were twice that for unpredictable static stimuli.
claims.source: In a comparison of between-subject multivariate pattern classification (bsMVPC) of responses to dynamic stimuli in movies to bsMVPC of responses to static stimuli in controlled experiments, with the structure of these analyses carefully matched to allow meaningful comparison, bsMVPC accuracies in ventral temporal extrastriate visual cortex for naturalistic, dynamic stimuli were twice that for unpredictable static stimuli (Supplemental Figure 4A in Haxby et al., 2011)
claims.evidence: This is a specific finding from Haxby et al., 2011.

claims.claim: A common model space can be built by estimating transformation matrices from fMRI data collected in the resting state using connectivity hyperalignment.
claims.source: A common model space also can be built by estimating transformation matrices from fMRI data collected in the resting state (rs-fMRI) using connectivity hyperalignment (Guntupalli et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Guntupalli et al., 2016.

claims.claim: A common model based on rs-fMRI data greatly increases intersubject correlations of functional connectivity indices and captures the fine-scale spatial structure of variation in connectivity.
claims.source: Such a model greatly increases intersubject correlations of functional connectivity indices and captures the fine-scale spatial structure of variation in connectivity that is seen in individual data.
claims.evidence: This describes the effectiveness of resting-state based hyperalignment.

claims.claim: The general validity of a common model based on rs-fMRI data for aligning brain states associated with a wide variety of stimuli and cognitive processes has not yet been established.
claims.source: The general validity of a common model based on rs-fMRI data for aligning brain states associated with a wide variety of stimuli and cognitive processes has not yet been established.
claims.evidence: This acknowledges a limitation of current knowledge.

claims.claim: Previous models of cortical functional architecture have focused on the division of cortex into contiguous functional areas.
claims.source: Previous models of cortical functional architecture have focused on the division of cortex into contiguous functional areas (Brodman, 1909; Glasser et al., 2016; Gordon et al., 2016; Shen et al., 2013; Shen et al., 2010; Yeo et al., 2011; Zilles and Amunts, 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on cortical parcellation.

claims.claim: Cortical parcellations may vary substantially across functional brain state and individuals.
claims.source: These parcellations, however, may vary substantially across functional brain state (Salehi et al., 2020) and individuals (Braga and Buckner, 2017; Gordon et al., 2017; Kong et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent work.

claims.claim: The conceptual framework for hyperalignment proposes a radically different basis for cortical topographies that is based on overlapping topographic basis functions.
claims.source: The conceptual framework for hyperalignment proposes a radically different basis for cortical topographies that is based on overlapping topographic basis functions, offering a model that accounts for individual variation in both fine-scale topographies and coarse-scale areal structure.
claims.evidence: This describes the novel contribution of the hyperalignment framework.

claims.claim: Each column in an individual transformation matrix is a pattern vector of weights for cortical loci in an individual subject's brain that serves as a topographic basis function.
claims.source: Each column in an individual transformation matrix (Ri) (or row in the transpose of that matrix, RiT), is a pattern vector of weights for cortical loci in an individual subject's brain. These pattern vectors for model dimensions serve as topographic basis functions.
claims.evidence: This describes how transformation matrices define basis functions.

claims.claim: Patterns that specify an area or topographic pattern in other subjects' cortex can be transformed into a group mean pattern in the common model information space.
claims.source: Patterns that specify an area or topographic pattern, such as a face-responsive area or retinopy, in other subjects' cortex (tp(B)) can be transformed into a group mean pattern in the common model information space (tp(M)) using their transformation matrices
claims.evidence: This describes how group patterns can be derived in the common space.

claims.claim: The mean topographic pattern in the model space can be projected into a new individual's cortical space using that individual's transformation matrix.
claims.source: The mean topographic pattern in the model space (tp(M)) can then be projected into a new individual's cortical space using that individual's transformation matrix and Equation 2, providing an estimate of that pattern (t̂p(Bi)) in that individual's brain.
claims.evidence: This describes how patterns can be transferred to new individuals.

claims.claim: Assessing the performance of hyperalignment requires testing on data that play no role in calculating the parameters in the transformation matrices.
claims.source: Assessing the performance of hyperalignment for modeling shared information and idiosyncratic topographies requires testing on data that play no role in calculating the parameters in the transformation matrices (Kriegeskorte et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is a standard principle of cross-validation, supported by citation.

claims.claim: Numerous tests with different data sets have shown marked and robust improvement of intersubject similarity on all indices after hyperalignment.
claims.source: Numerous tests with different data sets have shown marked and robust improvement of intersubject similarity on all of these indices (e.g., Chen et al., 2015; Guntupalli et al., 2018; Guntupalli et al., 2016; Haxby et al., 2011; Nastase et al., 2017; Van Uden et al., 2018)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: The magnitude of the beneficial effect of hyperalignment on bsMVPC is largest for small and moderately-sized ROIs which contain fine-scale topographies with minimal coarse-scale variation.
claims.source: The magnitude of the beneficial effect of hyperalignment on bsMVPC is largest for small and moderately-sized ROIs which contain fine-scale topographies with minimal coarse-scale variation, where bsMVPC accuracies for anatomically-aligned data are very low.
claims.evidence: This describes a pattern in the results.

claims.claim: In small cortical regions, hyperalignment provides more than a full order of magnitude improvement in bsMVPC.
claims.source: In small cortical regions, where accuracies for unsmoothed, anatomically aligned data are very low, hyperalignment provides more than a full order of magnitude improvement in bsMVPC (Guntupalli et al., 2018; Guntupalli et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is a specific finding supported by citations.

claims.claim: Response hyperalignment nearly doubled ISCs of time-series responses to a naturalistic movie.
claims.source: For example, response hyperalignment nearly doubled ISCs of time-series responses to a naturalistic movie (Guntupalli et al., 2016)
claims.evidence: This is a specific finding supported by citation.

claims.claim: ISC increases were even greater for functional connectivity profiles after connectivity hyperalignment.
claims.source: ISC increases were even greater for functional connectivity profiles after connectivity hyperalignment, for both functional connectivities measured during movie viewing and during the resting state (Figure 6; see Guntupalli et al., 2018, for details).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation and reference to Figure 6.

claims.claim: Searchlight-based whole-cortex hyperalignment greatly increases ISCs of local representational geometry.
claims.source: Searchlight-based whole-cortex hyperalignment greatly increases ISCs of local representational geometry (Figure 5b; Guntupalli et al., 2018; Guntupalli et al., 2016; Nastase et al., 2017; Van Uden et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations and reference to Figure 5b.

claims.claim: For naturalistic movies, hyperalignment increased mean ISC of representational geometry across searchlights by 46% to 75%.
claims.source: For naturalistic movies, hyperalignment increased mean ISC of representational geometry across searchlights by 46% to 75% (Guntupalli et al., 2016; Van Uden et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a specific finding supported by citations.

claims.claim: ROI hyperalignment does not change the vector geometry for each individual and has no effect on ISC of vector geometry.
claims.source: Indeed, ROI hyperalignment does not change the vector geometry for each individual and, therefore, has no effect on ISC of vector geometry.
claims.evidence: This is a logical consequence of the properties of ROI hyperalignment.

claims.claim: Searchlight hyperalignment resamples information into and out of local cortical fields, thereby increasing the similarity of local information content across subjects.
claims.source: Searchlight hyperalignment, by contrast, resamples information into and out of local cortical fields, thereby increasing the similarity of local information content across subjects.
claims.evidence: This explains the mechanism by which searchlight hyperalignment increases ISC of vector geometry.

claims.claim: The dissimilarity of vector geometry for overlapping cortical fields is substantial.
claims.source: The size of the increase suggests this is a large effect and that the dissimilarity of vector geometry for overlapping cortical fields is substantial.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the magnitude of ISC increases.

claims.claim: Between-subject MVPC of responses to still images after data were projected into a common space based on responses to a movie was equivalent to or better than within-subject MVPC.
claims.source: For example, bsMVPC of responses to still images of objects, faces, and animals after data were projected into a common space based on responses to a movie was equivalent to or better than within-subject MVPC (Guntupalli et al., 2016; Haxby et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is a specific finding supported by citations.

claims.claim: Higher bsMVPC than within-subject MVPC of hyperaligned data demonstrated the added power of using large multi-subject data sets for training a pattern classifier.
claims.source: Higher bsMVPC than within-subject MVPC of hyperaligned data demonstrated the added power of using large multi-subject data sets for training a pattern classifier, which hyperalignment makes possible.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the finding that bsMVPC can exceed within-subject MVPC.

claims.claim: ISC of representational geometry for responses to brief video clips were greatly increased after data were projected into a common space based on responses to a continuous movie.
claims.source: Similarly, ISC of representational geometry for responses to brief video clips of different categories of animals performing different actions were greatly increased after data were projected into a common space based on responses to a continuous movie (Nastase et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is a specific finding supported by citation.

claims.claim: Connectivity hyperalignment makes it possible to derive transformation matrices to project new subjects' cortical space into a model space using connectivity data from experimental paradigms that differ from the experimental paradigm used to derive that common model space.
claims.source: Moreover, connectivity hyperalignment now makes it possible to derive transformation matrices to project new subjects' cortical space into a model space using connectivity data from experimental paradigms (e.g., a movie or the resting state) that differ from the experimental paradigm used to derive that common model space (Guntupalli et al., 2018; Nastase et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations.

claims.claim: Hyperalignment made it possible to create a response pattern template based on other subjects' hyperaligned data for use in new subjects who were never exposed to the stimulus as a target brain state for neurofeedback.
claims.source: In a novel application (Taschereau-Dumouchel et al., 2018), hyperalignment made it possible to create a response pattern template based on other subjects' hyperaligned data for use in new subjects who were never exposed to the stimulus as a target brain state for neurofeedback.
claims.evidence: This is a specific application supported by citation.

claims.claim: Response hyperalignment and connectivity hyperalignment both produce transformation matrices that project data from cortical coordinate spaces into a common model information space.
claims.source: Response and connectivity hyperalignment both produce transformation matrices that project data from cortical coordinate spaces into a common model information space.
claims.evidence: This describes a commonality between the two approaches.

claims.claim: The two algorithms align the vector geometries for related, but distinct types of information – patterns of responses and patterns of connectivity.
claims.source: The two algorithms align the vector geometries for related, but distinct types of information – patterns of responses and patterns of connectivity.

results.result: Hyperalignment models shared information across brains by projecting idiosyncratic cortical topographies into a common high-dimensional information space, preserving information content (vector geometry) while remixing functional profiles of individual units. This framework posits that information content, rather than functional properties of local features, is the fundamental property preserved across brains.
results.evaluation: This core conceptual framework is well-supported by the mathematical formulation (C2, C3, C25), extensive empirical validation showing preservation of vector geometry (C72-C96), and consistent theoretical reasoning throughout (C132-C137). The claims are mutually reinforcing and supported by both computational methods and experimental data.

results.result: Whole-cortex searchlight hyperalignment uses Generalized Procrustes Analysis to derive transformation matrices from overlapping searchlights, preserving local vector geometry through rigid rotations while avoiding remixing information from distant cortical locations. This approach produces overlapping topographic basis functions constrained by searchlight size rather than areal boundaries.
results.evaluation: The mathematical properties of Procrustes transformations (C34-C36) are well-established, and the searchlight implementation (C40-C42) is supported by citations and empirical validation. The claim that this preserves local vector geometry better than alternatives is supported by comparative data (C39).

results.result: Hyperalignment produces marked improvements across multiple validation metrics: bsMVPC accuracies increase by more than an order of magnitude in small ROIs, ISCs of response profiles nearly double, and ISCs of representational geometry increase by 46-75%. Performance can equal or exceed within-subject classification, demonstrating the power of multi-subject datasets.
results.evaluation: These performance claims are supported by multiple independent datasets (C72) with specific quantitative results (C74-C78, C82). The findings are consistent across different validation approaches and are supported by references to figures and citations. The magnitude of improvements is substantial and well-documented.

results.result: Connectivity hyperalignment aligns fine-scale connectome structure across subjects without requiring common stimuli, enabling resting-state hyperalignment. While response and connectivity hyperalignment produce related but non-equivalent common spaces, transformations from either approach can align both response and connectivity data, with each performing best for its target data type.
results.evaluation: The claims about connectivity hyperalignment are well-supported by citations (C48-C52) and quantitative comparisons (C91-C96, Table 1). The finding that the two approaches produce related but distinct spaces is supported by specific ISC values showing differential performance. The cross-applicability is empirically demonstrated.

results.result: Individual-specific functional topographies including retinotopy and category-selective regions can be estimated with high fidelity (correlations >0.80) from other subjects' data. PCA analysis reveals that approximately 35 dimensions capture movie response information, with traditional face-versus-object distinctions accounting for only 7% of variance compared to 22% for the first PC alone.
results.evaluation: The high-fidelity estimation claims are supported by specific correlation values (C98) and visual evidence in Figures 7-8 (C97). The PCA analysis provides specific quantitative findings (C99-C106) that challenge traditional views of cortical organization. The cross-validated variance estimates strengthen these claims.

results.result: Spatial point-spread function analysis demonstrates that hyperalignment preserves functional profile distinctiveness at single voxel/vertex granularity (~3mm) across all tested cortical regions. The dramatically steeper PSF after hyperalignment compared to anatomical alignment reveals fine-grained connectome structure not previously recognized.
results.evaluation: The PSF analysis provides direct quantitative evidence (C107-C111, Figure 9) for fine-scale preservation. The within-subject PSF equivalence to between-subject PSF (C111) provides strong validation. The generality across cortical regions (C110) strengthens the claim, though the novelty claim (C112) is somewhat speculative.

results.result: Hyperalignment increases the reliability of individual differences despite reducing their magnitude, with this increased reliability attributable to fine-scale topographic information. Fine-scale individual differences are more predictive of cognitive abilities like general intelligence than coarse-scale differences, and hyperalignment enables investigation of these differences while factoring out topographic misalignment.
results.evaluation: The counterintuitive finding of increased reliability despite reduced magnitude (C113) is well-supported by data in Figure 10. The decomposition into coarse and fine-scale components (C114-C116) provides mechanistic insight. The predictive validity for intelligence (C117) is supported by citation, though this represents a single cognitive measure.

results.result: Naturalistic movie stimuli provide rich sampling of cortical patterns necessary for effective hyperalignment, with transformation matrices showing general validity across experiments. Movies evoke twice the bsMVPC accuracy of static stimuli in controlled experiments. Resting-state connectivity hyperalignment is possible but its general validity across diverse tasks remains unestablished.
results.evaluation: The requirement for rich stimuli (C53) is supported by comparative data (C54-C55, C60). The advantages of movies are well-reasoned (C56-C59) and empirically demonstrated (C60). The acknowledgment of uncertainty about resting-state generalizability (C63) is appropriately cautious given current evidence.

results.result: Hyperalignment proposes a radically different model of cortical functional architecture based on overlapping topographic basis functions rather than contiguous functional areas. While the model can identify areal boundaries, topographic information is not strongly constrained by these boundaries, suggesting areal structure plays a smaller role than previously believed.
results.evaluation: The conceptual framework (C66-C70) is clearly articulated and supported by the PCA analysis showing limited variance explained by traditional areal distinctions (C15, C100-C106). The challenge to traditional parcellation approaches (C64-C65) is supported by citations. However, the claim about areal structure's reduced role (C16) is somewhat inferential.

results.result: Dimensionality reduction of the common model space using PCA can preserve or improve performance despite necessarily warping vector geometry, effectively denoising data. Regularized CCA with relaxed orthogonality constraints also enhances performance.
results.evaluation: The claims about PCA dimensionality reduction (C44-C46) are supported by citations and represent a well-understood trade-off between noise reduction and geometry preservation. The rCCA finding (C47) is presented as the authors' own result but lacks detailed quantitative support in this manuscript.

results.result: ROI hyperalignment preserves individual vector geometry and has no effect on ISC of vector geometry, while searchlight hyperalignment resamples information into and out of local cortical fields, increasing similarity of local information content. The magnitude of ISC increases suggests substantial dissimilarity of vector geometry for overlapping cortical fields.
results.evaluation: The distinction between ROI and searchlight approaches (C79-C80) follows logically from their mathematical properties. The inference about substantial dissimilarity (C81) is reasonable given the 46-75% increases in ISC, though this is an indirect measure.

results.result: Other approaches to modeling shared cortical information have limitations: most focus on areal structure and overlook fine-scale patterns; RSA and pattern component modeling treat topographies as unimportant and lack methods for modeling idiosyncrasies; forward encoding predefines shared information by stimulus features and doesn't investigate population codes with representational geometry.
results.evaluation: The characterization of alternative approaches (C121-C131) is generally fair and supported by citations. The limitations identified are logical consequences of each method's design. However, some claims about what methods "do not attempt" (C126, C130, C131) may be overstated, as these could be extensions rather than fundamental limitations.

results.result: Traditional neuroscience focuses on individual unit profiles as primary with population information as secondary, but hyperalignment results suggest unit profiles are shaped to support information geometry rather than geometry being merely a reflection of unit profiles. Unit profiles develop with experience, show complexity, may fluctuate over time, and need not be easily interpretable, while supporting consistent population-level information.
results.evaluation: The contrast with traditional approaches (C136) is well-supported by citations. The reinterpretation (C137) is a reasonable inference from hyperalignment results. The supporting claims about unit profile properties (C138-C145) are backed by appropriate citations. However, the mechanistic claims about learning (C147) are more speculative.

results.result: Hyperalignment models cortical functional architecture as a degenerate biological system where structurally different elements perform the same function. This parallels deep neural networks where individual features vary but information content is preserved, and linguistic systems where meaning is preserved across variable surface structure. Degeneracy enables emergence of new functions and provides basis for evolution and individual cognitive diversity.

The analogies to CNNs (C148-C149) and language (C150-C151) are appropriate and supported. The general properties of degenerate systems (C153-C156) are well-established. results.result: The hyperalignment framework defines information as relationships among pattern vectors in high-dimensional spaces, with this geometric framework used across multiple fields. The common model space has dimensions that are weighted sums of anatomical locations, not one-to-one mappings, with individual-specific weight distributions. Model dimensionality can match a reference brain or be reduced for denoising.

Hyperalignment has been successfully applied to neurofeedback using templates from other subjects.
